## Airlift v0.3.6

### ✨ Drops joins the catalog
- Send a file to your other device from a window or the tray. Drag it in, paste it, or send the clipboard; everything deletes itself after an hour. Listed under Utilities.

### ✨ Forge 2 installers
- Airlift now reads installers built with Forge 2 as well as Forge 1 when it checks a download's identity and version.

### ✨ Catalog refresh
- The shelf now holds nineteen apps.

## Airlift v0.3.5

### ✨ Beetle joins the catalog
- Control an ELK-BLEDOM Bluetooth LED strip from your PC: colour, brightness, and ambient, rainbow and music modes, from the tray. Listed under Utilities.

### ✨ Lounge joins the catalog
- A media center you drive with an Xbox controller: films, music, streaming, apps and files, in five themes, without a keyboard or mouse. Listed under Media.

### ✨ Catalog refresh
- The shelf now holds eighteen apps.

## Airlift v0.3.4

### ✨ Tarman joins the catalog
- A task manager and resource monitor that keeps ten minutes of history, so you can scroll back to a spike and find the process behind it. Listed under Utilities.

### ✨ Qemik joins the catalog
- A native QEMU desktop: create a Linux workspace, keep a Windows sandbox, or give an old system another life. Listed under Developer tools.

### ✨ Catalog refresh
- The shelf now holds sixteen apps.
- Versions catch up with their manifests: Descry 0.92.0, Atelier 0.5.0, clockt 0.5.26, Gitland 0.14.2, Hisashi 0.6.29, Cogas 0.19.1, osXos 0.2.5, Sir Word-a-lot 0.1.5 and HammerOS 0.3.5.

## Airlift v0.3.3

### ✨ Open app, for every app you have installed

- **Sir Word-a-lot** offered no way to open it. Airlift looked for the program under the app's display name, and `Sir Word-a-lot.exe` is not what the app installs, so the button was simply never drawn.
- Airlift now looks for the program under the app's name, then the project it is built from, and finally the icon recorded by its uninstaller when that points at a program inside the installation. Nothing outside the installed folder is ever opened.
- Every other app was unaffected only by luck: Windows matches file names without regard to case.

### ✨ See repo

- **Manage** now carries **See repo**, which opens the app's GitHub repository, beside **Open app**. It is there for every app, installed or not.

## Airlift v0.3.2

### ✨ HammerOS joins the catalog

- **HammerOS** is on the shelf: a fullscreen retro workspace with your real files, independent shells, and Windows apps embedded in one tiled screen. Fourteen apps now.
- It accepted the invitation in 0.3.1 but had no repository to follow yet, so the catalog listed it as waiting. It was published minutes after 0.3.1 went out, and this is the first catalog built since.
- Sir Word-a-lot follows its own 0.1.2.

## Airlift v0.3.1

### ✨ Sir Word-a-lot joins the catalog

- **Sir Word-a-lot** is on the shelf: a vocabulary and thesaurus trainer that keeps a word with the sentence you met it in, enriches it with real synonyms, and brings it back until it sticks. Thirteen apps now.
- Four apps caught up with their current builds: clockt 0.5.24, Gitland 0.14.0, Hisashi 0.6.17 and osXos 0.2.1.

### ✨ Apps invite Airlift in

- An app joins the catalog by saying so, in a `properties.piml` at the root of its repository holding `(airlift) true`. Airlift used to sweep up every neighbouring project that happened to carry an installer manifest, and keep a hand-written list of the ones to leave alone.
- A project that has invited Airlift but has not been published yet is named as waiting rather than breaking the import. It appears on the shelf the first time the catalog is rebuilt after its first release.

### ✨ An app is installable whatever it is called

- Airlift looked for a Windows installer named after the app, which holds until an app's name is not a file name. Sir Word-a-lot publishes `SirWordALot-Setup-0.1.1.exe`, and Airlift would have reported its release as having no package for Windows. It now follows the project, so the app installs and updates like any other.

## Airlift v0.3.0

### ✨ Two themes, and room for more

- **Meadow** is the Airlift you know: warm greens. **Altitude** is new — cool blues, high and clear. Choose one under **Settings → Appearance**, and Airlift remembers it.
- The whole interface changes, not just the highlight colour: surfaces, borders, type and the Discover hero all move together, at matching lightness so nothing becomes harder to read.
- The Airlift mark keeps its green in both themes, and every app in your catalog keeps its own colour.
- Warnings and the close button look the same whichever theme is on, because they mean something rather than decorate.
- Every colour in the app now has a name rather than a value, so a future theme is a list of colours and appears in Settings on its own.

### ✨ A failed release check says so

- When GitHub refuses a check — usually its limit on how often an app may ask without signing in — the reason now appears in the status bar, and a check you asked for also opens a dialog explaining the limit, when to try again, and what Airlift is still showing you.
- Background checks stay quiet. Only a check you started interrupts you.

## Airlift v0.2.10

### ✨ A release check that admits when it could not run

- GitHub limits how many times an app may ask about releases in an hour. Once that limit pauses Airlift's requests, the pause is now recorded rather than quietly discarded.
- Before this, a paused check looked exactly like a successful one. Airlift would say "You're running the latest Airlift version" while holding release information from well before the newest version, and the Sources page reported that every repository had been checked.
- Airlift now tells you the check could not run and shows you the time it can try again, keeping whatever it already knew. The next check that reaches GitHub clears the message.

## Airlift v0.2.9

### ✨ A details dialog you can actually read

- Release notes and app facts keep a gutter clear for the scrollbar, so the version, repository and download values are no longer printed underneath it.
- Markdown headings are given a line box sized for their own type. A release note titled with a large heading used to lose the top and bottom of every letter.

### ✨ Find what you do not already have

- Discover gained a **Hide installed** switch, so the catalog can show only the apps that are not on this computer yet. My library and Updates leave it out, since listing installed apps is their whole job.
- The search box now has a clear button inside it, and Escape empties it too.

### ✨ A window that moves from the top of the sidebar

- Dragging the Airlift mark and the panel around it moves the window, which it was meant to do since the custom frame arrived in 0.2.7.

### ✨ Built and released from one place

- The GitHub Actions workflow is gone. Airlift is built, tested and published from a single machine, and the local build with its tests is the gate before a release.

## Airlift v0.2.8

### ✨ Gitland joins the catalog

- Gitland, the native Git client built around readable diffs, three-way review and an editable merge result, is now tracked from `fezcode/gitland`.
- It carries its own branch-and-island mark, and Airlift follows its public releases alongside every other app in the workspace.
- Gitland currently publishes a zip rather than a Forge installer, so its card opens Details and Sources lists the release. Installing from Airlift begins the moment a Setup executable is published.

### ✨ A catalog that only lists what it can follow

- The workspace import now holds back projects that carry a Forge manifest but have not published a release, so Airlift never shows an app whose every release check would go unanswered.

### ✨ Refreshed catalog

- Versions and icons for the already catalogued apps were refreshed from their current Forge manifests, including a new clockt icon.

## Airlift v0.2.7

### ✨ Airlift's own window frame

- Every Airlift window now draws its own title bar, with minimize, maximize and close glyphs styled to match the app instead of the operating system's frame.
- Windows keeps what it does best: resizable edges, drop shadow, Aero Snap, and the Windows 11 snap layouts flyout on the maximize button.
- Drag the window by its title strip or by the sidebar's Airlift mark, and double-click the strip to maximize.
- A maximized window widens its content gutters so the layout breathes, and steps inside the off-screen resize border rather than letting its edges be clipped.
- App details and confirmation dialogs wear the same frame.

### ✨ A sidebar footer that tells you something

- The decorative profile chip is gone. In its place, the running Airlift version and a live status line: up to date, an available release, or a check in progress.
- When a newer Airlift release is waiting, the card is lit and takes you straight to Updates.

### ✨ Support Airlift

- Settings gained a Support Airlift card with a one-click star on GitHub and a link for reporting issues.

## Airlift v0.2.6

### ✨ Clear old installers
- Review and remove cached Forge installers that are older than the installed version of their app, from **Settings → Installer cache** or the **Downloads** header.
- Airlift's own superseded installers are included, so the cache no longer grows with every self-update.
- A preview shows how many installers and how much space would be freed before anything is deleted.

### ✨ Careful by default
- Only completed installers whose embedded Forge identity matches the owning app are eligible.
- Current versions, newer updates, unknown or unreadable files, unfinished downloads, apps with an active operation and any linked path are kept.
- Eligibility is rechecked under the package operation lock after the preview, so a stale preview is never deletion authority on its own.
- Cleanup stays inside Airlift's own download cache; Windows temp folders and user settings are never swept.

### ✨ Validation
- 59 native tests passed, including new installer-cache eligibility and safety regressions.
- Setup packaging verified the bundle checksum, six wizard steps, MIT license, shortcuts, registry values, folder payload and finish launch.

## Airlift v0.2.5

### ✨ Optional silent updates
- Choose silent installation when updating a managed Windows app. The setup wizard remains the default, and fresh installations always use it.
- Update Airlift silently with a clean shutdown and automatic restart after successful installation.
- Preserve the existing installation folder, verify downloads, and reject missing installations or downgrades.
- Use `airlift-cli update <app> --silent` from the command line.

### ✨ Accurate installed versions
- Refresh installed versions after package operations and when returning to Airlift.
- Prevent an older inventory refresh from overwriting a completed update, keeping version labels and update counts consistent.

### ✨ A sidebar that fits
- Scroll navigation independently at smaller window heights, keeping Settings and the profile clear of other items.

### ✨ Complete Windows setup
- Include all six Mica wizard steps, the MIT license agreement, and optional Desktop and Start Menu shortcuts.
- Register Airlift's installation folder and version, and use its dedicated icon for shortcuts.
- Ship the desktop app and CLI as self-contained folders with their required libraries.

### ✨ Validation
- 53 native tests passed, including UI and update regressions.
- Forge runtime tests and the disposable install, silent upgrade, and uninstall test passed.

## What's new

### See it in action
The README now opens with a short demo video: flipping through a folder with the arrow keys, zooming right into the detail, an SVG staying razor sharp at any zoom, and rotating with **R**.

### Glass installer
Setup now uses a frosted glass look that matches Atelier's own glass theme.

## Install
Download `Atelier-Setup-0.7.2.exe` below and run it.

## What's new

### Crop tool
A proper crop tool in edit mode, modelled on Preview's:

- Press **C**, click the **Crop** button in the ribbon, or choose **Image > Crop...**
- A frame appears round the picture (or round your selection, if you had one)
- Drag the corners or edges to resize, drag inside to move, drag outside to draw a new frame
- The area outside the frame is dimmed, with a rule-of-thirds grid and a live pixel-size readout
- Aspect presets: Freeform, Original, 1:1, 4:3, 3:2, 16:9 and portrait variants; hold **Shift** to keep the current shape
- **Enter** crops, **Esc** resets the frame, **Ctrl+Z** undoes

### Copy Path
**Edit > Copy Path** (**Ctrl+Shift+C**) copies the image's full file path as text.

## Install
Download `Atelier-Setup-0.7.1.exe` below and run it.

## A new look

Atelier now sits on glass taken from its icon: dark violet panes over Windows 11 Mica, with a faint iridescent sheen.

- **View > Appearance** (Ctrl+, or the Appearance button in the title bar) tunes it live:
  - **Material:** Mica, Acrylic, Blur or Solid
  - **Tint:** seven colours from the icon, plus a hue slider
  - **Glassiness, Transparency and Colour level** sliders
- Redesigned top bar, metadata pane, editing toolbar, a floating navigation dock, a new empty-window screen, and every dialog
- Cleaner text on glass, and shortcut labels written the way you type them (Ctrl+, instead of Ctrl+OemComma)

## Faster first launch

The app no longer embeds images it never shows, so its main DLL is 1.7 MB instead of 9.2 MB.

## Install

Download **Atelier-Setup-0.7.0.exe** below.

## Atelier v0.6.1

### Refreshed application icon

- Apply the approved icon design with a transparent background and crisp sizes for Windows shortcuts and taskbars.
- Keep executable and runtime artwork consistent, with the approved master and reproducible asset exporter in the repository.

### Validation

- Windows release build and required checks passed. The installer and payload contain all seven approved icon frames, with transparency preserved.

## What's new

### EXIF and Content Credentials in the metadata pane
The pane is now split into **File**, **EXIF** and **Content Credentials (C2PA)**.
- EXIF is grouped by directory (camera & image, capture, GPS with coordinates, interoperability).
- C2PA shows who signed the picture, when, which app or device made it, whether it came from generative AI, what was done to it and what it was made from. Read from JPEG, PNG, WebP, HEIF/AVIF and `.c2pa` sidecars; remote manifests show their URL. Signatures are displayed, not verified.

### Remove Metadata
**File → Remove Metadata** (or the button under the pane) strips EXIF, XMP, IPTC, comments and C2PA, in place or to a clean copy. JPEG, PNG and WebP are rewritten without re-encoding, so the pixels are untouched; the colour profile and orientation are kept.

### Save As in 32 formats
PNG, JPEG, WebP, AVIF, JPEG XL, TIFF, BMP, GIF, ICO, JPEG 2000, QOI, PSD, TGA, DDS, OpenEXR, Radiance HDR, PDF, EPS, the Netpbm family, PCX, SGI, Sun Raster, XPM, XBM, WBMP, FITS, Farbfeld and MIFF. Everything except PDF and EPS reopens in Atelier. HEIC was dropped from Save As: the bundled encoder never supported writing it.

### Crisper text
The interface now uses Segoe UI. The previous font always rendered at its thinnest weight.

﻿## Paint-style editing

**Edit → Edit Image** now opens a Paint ribbon over the picture. The brightness, saturation, hue, contrast and blur sliders and the filters are still there, applied on top of your painting until you save.

- **Tools:** pencil, fill (with an optional tolerance), text (font, size, bold, italic, underline, strikethrough, opaque background), eraser (right-drag replaces colour 1 with colour 2), colour picker, magnifier.
- **Brushes:** brush, two calligraphy brushes, airbrush, oil, crayon, marker, natural pencil, watercolour.
- **Shapes:** all 23 of Paint's, including line, curve, polygon, arrows, stars, callouts, heart and lightning. Outline and fill can each be on or off; Shift gives perfect squares, circles and 45° lines.
- **Selection:** rectangular or free-form. Move it, Ctrl+drag to copy, nudge with the arrow keys, select all, invert, delete, crop, cut, copy and paste, plus transparent selection.
- **Image:** resize and skew, canvas size, rotate, flip, invert colours, gridlines.
- **Colours:** colour 1 and colour 2, Paint's palette, custom colours and an Edit Colours picker.
- **Undo and redo** for everything, Paint's keyboard shortcuts, and a status bar showing pointer position, selection size, canvas size and zoom.

Saving keeps the photo's EXIF data and colour profile. A photo turned by its camera tag is edited the way up it is shown, and saved upright.

### Behaviour changes while editing
- **Delete** clears the selection. It never sends the file to the Recycle Bin while you are editing.
- The **arrow keys** move the selection instead of going to the next picture.
- Opening another picture or closing with unsaved edits asks before discarding them.

### Fixed
- The Invert filter also inverted transparency, which could save a photo as fully transparent.

Photos that carry an EXIF orientation tag no longer open on their side — and rotating, copying, renaming, deleting and animation arrive alongside the fix.

## Photos land the right way up

Avalonia's decoder ignores the EXIF orientation tag, so a portrait phone photo has always opened sideways in Atelier. That is fixed as part of rotation rather than beside it: all eight EXIF orientations and every rotate and flip are one value, and the tag is simply where that value starts.

Saving bakes the turn into the pixels *and* clears the tag — leave the tag behind and the next open turns the picture another 90°.

## Rotate and flip

**Edit → Rotate Right / Rotate Left** (`R`, `Shift+R`) and **Flip Horizontal / Vertical**.

Rotation is non-destructive. The picture turns on screen and nothing reaches the disk until you save, with a prompt before you navigate away from an unsaved turn.

## Clipboard

**Ctrl+C** puts the picture on the clipboard as pixels, as the file and as its path at once — so it pastes into Paint, an Explorer window and a text box alike.

**Ctrl+V** opens an image from the clipboard, preferring a copied file over loose pixels so you keep the original rather than a re-encode.

## Rename and delete

**F2** renames, keeping the extension if you type a bare name.

**Del** moves the picture to the Recycle Bin and shows the next one. There is no permanent delete — Del sits next to the arrow keys you navigate with, so a mis-tap stays recoverable.

## Animated GIF and WebP

Animations play at the frame delays the file asks for, and **Space** pauses. Files are measured before decoding, so a very long animation falls back to a still first frame instead of filling memory.

GIF and AVIF also join the formats Next/Prev will walk to — Atelier could always display them, so skipping them was a gap rather than a decision.

## Zoom

`Ctrl+0` fits to the window, `Ctrl+1` is actual size, `Ctrl+±` steps the zoom.

## Note on an existing shortcut

**Ctrl+S now saves the picture**, since a rotation can leave it unsaved. **Save As has moved to Ctrl+Shift+S.**

Edit Image is unavailable for animated files, which a save would otherwise flatten to a single frame.

98 new headless tests, 199 in total.

**Install:** download `Atelier-Setup-0.4.0.exe` below and run it.

## Next and Previous now follow the order Explorer is showing

Open the top picture of a folder sorted newest-first and press Next, and Atelier
used to jump to whatever came next in the alphabet — its sibling list was a plain
alphabetical sort of the folder, no matter how the folder looked on screen.

Atelier now reads the item order straight out of the Explorer window showing that
folder, so navigation follows that window's sort, its grouping, and any filter
applied to it. Re-sort the window and the next picture you open picks the new
order up — no restart.

Reading the view's *order* rather than its sort column is deliberate. A pictures
folder is typically sorted by the shell's composite "Date" column, whose value is
date-taken for some files and date-modified for others; there is no faithful way
to reimplement that, and the view already has the answer.

Navigation falls back to the previous alphabetical order whenever that window
cannot be asked — Atelier launched from Run or from another app, the folder window
closed since, or a searching view that is not showing the picture you have open.

## A hidden Image Info pane gives its width back

Launching with the Image Info pane turned off still reserved its 300px column, so
the viewer opened with an empty dark strip down the right edge that looked exactly
like the pane it had been told to hide. The image now uses the full window.

over any earlier Forge-built install.

Installer rebuilt with [Forge](https://github.com/fezcode/Forge) 1.4.0 — no Atelier changes since 0.3.2.

### Installing over an existing copy
- Shortcuts are now written natively (IShellLinkW) and always built from scratch instead of rewriting the existing `.lnk`, so repair, reinstall and upgrade over an existing Atelier install complete cleanly. This is the path Forge 1.3.0 broke: `IPropertyStore.SetValue: Incorrect function` aborted the install mid-way and the rollback then removed the previous copy.
- The install record (`installed_files.json`) is staged and committed only when the install succeeds, so a failed run can no longer corrupt the previous install's record.

### Uninstall that never dead-ends
- An `uninstall.json` plan records the install folder, shortcuts, registry keys and environment edits. If the install record is missing or partial, removal is reconstructed from the plan or the embedded manifest, and the Add/Remove Programs entry (both hives) and plan artifacts are always swept.
- Stale Add/Remove Programs entries whose install folder is gone are cleaned up automatically and treated as a fresh install.
- Per-user uninstalls no longer show a UAC prompt — `uninstall.exe` elevates only when the install actually needs it (per-machine / Program Files).

### Housekeeping
- The wizard's WebView2 profile lives in `%TEMP%\forge-webview\<app id>` and is removed on exit, instead of leaving a `%APPDATA%\<Setup exe name>\` folder behind for every version.
- The install directory is validated (absolute, not a protected root), wizard errors are shown in a message box, and `--dir` works for GUI installs too.

An existing 0.3.2 install still carries the old uninstaller — install 0.3.3 over it and the new one takes over.

## Edit > Open with Paint

A new item in the Edit menu hands the file on disk straight to Microsoft Paint.

It is enabled only for the formats Paint can actually decode --- BMP, DIB, JPEG,
JFIF, GIF, PNG, TIFF, ICO and WebP. SVG and HEIC/HEIF stay greyed out: Paint has
no SVG support at all, and HEIC only decodes with the optional Store extension
installed, so either would have opened Paint onto an error.

Like Set as Wallpaper, it is unavailable while Edit Mode is active, where it
would silently miss the adjustments on screen.

## The Image Info pane remembers whether it is open

Closing the pane used to last only until the next launch. The choice now lives in
`%APPDATA%\fezcode\Atelier\settings.json` as `showMetadata`, alongside the Hisashi
switches, so a closed pane stays closed --- from the pane's own X button or from
View > Image Metadata.

## Also

- 89 headless Avalonia tests, up from 65.

Installer rebuilt with Forge 1.2.0 — no app changes since 0.3.0.

- Uninstaller: the Add/Remove Programs entry is removed from both registry hives, empty registry keys the installer created are pruned, shortcuts and emptied folders go with them, and a new **Also remove my settings and data** option purges `%APPDATA%\fezcode\Atelier` on request.
- **File associations are cleaned up**: the `Atelier*` ProgIDs written by *Set as default viewer*, their *Open with* entries and default-handler references are removed and Explorer is told to refresh, so no orphaned Atelier icons remain after uninstall.
- An existing 0.3.0 install still carries the old uninstaller — install 0.3.1 over it and the new one takes over.

Atelier's menus move into Hisashi's macOS-style menu bar.

### Hisashi menubar
With [Hisashi 0.5.1](https://github.com/fezcode/hisashi/releases/tag/v0.5.1) running, **View → Hisashi → Connect to Hisashi** (off by default) publishes File / View / Edit / Help to the bar over the hoswl named pipe — the same XAML menu the window draws, so shortcuts, greyed rows (Open File Location, Set as Wallpaper until an image is loaded), the Image Metadata checkmark and the Wallpaper submenu all come along, and stay in step as the view model changes. Picks arrive on the UI thread and drive the real menu items, so every existing handler is reused. The in-app strip hides and the top bar shrinks to the drag area while connected; **Show Menus in Hisashi** keeps the connection but leaves the menus in-app. If Hisashi quits, the strip is back at once and Atelier reconnects on its own when it returns.

Both switches are remembered in `%APPDATA%\fezcode\Atelier\settings.json` — Atelier's first settings file.

The client (`Hoswl/HoswlClient.cs`) is self-contained: no reference to Hisashi, no threads beyond one reader task, never blocks the UI.

### Build
`dotnet test Tests/Atelier.ZoomTests` now also covers the menu-tree builder, click dispatch, the strip hiding, and a full protocol round-trip against an in-test pipe server.

Per-user data moves into the shared Fezcode tree.

- The wallpaper cache moves from `%LOCALAPPDATA%\Atelier\Wallpaper` to `%APPDATA%\fezcode\Atelier\Wallpaper`.

**No migration.** The old folder is abandoned rather than read; a fresh cache is written the next time you apply a wallpaper. Delete `%LOCALAPPDATA%\Atelier` by hand if you want it gone.

## Atelier v0.2.85

### Atelier badge on Explorer thumbnails
- Image files associated with Atelier now show the Atelier logo in the bottom-right corner of their Explorer thumbnails, while keeping the image preview itself.
- Applies to types where Atelier is the **default** app. To pick it up on an existing install, open **File → File Associations** and save again.
- The badge appears wherever Explorer can render a thumbnail (PNG/JPEG always; HEIC/AVIF need the Windows codec extensions).

### Installer fix: drag-and-drop right after install
- The app launched from the installer's finish page used to inherit the installer's admin rights, and Windows silently blocks drag-and-drop from Explorer into elevated windows.
- The installer now starts Atelier as the normal desktop user, so dropping images works immediately after installing.

## Atelier v0.2.84

### Picture Frame mode, refined
- **Always on top** — a framed picture now stays above other windows until you exit frame mode.
- **Move the window** by dragging the top strip of the frame with the left mouse button.
- **Pan the image** by left-dragging anywhere below the top strip, as usual.
- **Zoom with the mouse wheel** — no Ctrl needed while framed; the wheel zooms around the cursor.
- The **EXIT FRAME** button disappears after 5 seconds; hover the top of the window to bring it back. **Esc** always exits.

## Atelier v0.2.83

### Fullscreen that is actually fullscreen
- Fullscreen now hides the menu bar, bottom bar and metadata pane — nothing on screen but the image.
- Enter with **F**, exit with **F** or **Esc**.
- Leaving fullscreen restores the window state you were in before (maximized stays maximized).

### New: Picture Frame mode
- **View → Picture Frame** strips the window down to the image plus the system minimize/maximize/close buttons.
- An **EXIT FRAME** button overlays the top-left corner; click it or press **Esc** to return to the normal layout.
- Pressing **F** in frame mode layers fullscreen on top; **Esc** unwinds one layer at a time.

## New

**Set as Wallpaper.** `File → Set as Wallpaper` sets the image you are viewing as your desktop background, with a choice of how it is positioned:

| | |
|---|---|
| **Fill** | Crops to cover the screen |
| **Fit** | Whole image, letterboxed |
| **Stretch** | Distorts to fill exactly |
| **Center** | Original size, centred |
| **Tile** | Repeats across the desktop |
| **Span** | One image across all monitors |

Windows only accepts JPG, PNG and BMP as a background, so **SVG, HEIC, AVIF, WebP, ICO and GIF are converted automatically** — no need to export first. SVG files are rasterised at your screen's resolution so they stay sharp, and multi-frame icons use their largest frame rather than a 16×16 thumbnail. Images Windows already understands are used directly, so *Settings → Personalization* still points at the original file.

The menu is unavailable while editing, since it uses the file on disk rather than unsaved adjustments. A short confirmation appears in the bottom bar once the wallpaper is applied.

## Fixed

**The editor could open invisibly.** If you closed the metadata panel with the ✕ added in v0.2.81 and then chose *Edit Image*, the panel holding the editing controls did not reappear.

**Full Changelog**: https://github.com/fezcode/Atelier/compare/v0.2.81...v0.2.82

## New

**Close the metadata panel from the panel itself.** The panel header now has an **✕** button, so you no longer have to go to *View → Image Metadata* to dismiss it. The menu item still works and is how you bring the panel back. The button is hidden while editing, where the panel holds the editor.

**File → Open File Location.** Reveals the image you are viewing in File Explorer with the file already selected. The menu item stays greyed out until an image is open, and falls back to opening the containing folder if the file has been moved or deleted since you opened it.

## Notes

Nothing else about the application changed, and the installer is unchanged from v0.2.80 — it uses the mica theme and installs to `C:\Program Files\Atelier`.

If you are coming from **v0.2.78 or earlier**, that version was built with a different installer that setup cannot detect; uninstall it first or let this one install over it at the same path. If you installed **v0.2.79**, delete `%LOCALAPPDATA%\Programs\Atelier` after upgrading, since that release briefly installed there.

**Full Changelog**: https://github.com/fezcode/Atelier/compare/v0.2.80...v0.2.81

Installer-only release. The application itself is unchanged from v0.2.79.

## Fixed

**The wizard showed a literal `${app.version}` instead of the version number.** [Forge](https://github.com/fezcode/Forge) expanded `${...}` placeholders in install paths, registry values and the window title, but not in wizard step text — themes render step titles and bodies verbatim. Fixed upstream in Forge; this release ships an installer built with the fix.

## Security

A full audit of the app, with every fix covered by tests:

- **Links** open only for `http`, `https` and `mailto`, after a prompt that shows the whole target. They never pass through a shell. On Linux and macOS a crafted link could previously run commands.
- **Network-path images** (`//host/share/x.png`) are no longer loaded. On Windows, simply viewing a note containing one could send your login hash to another machine.
- **Remote image fetches** never send Windows credentials or cookies. Set `remote_images = false` in `settings.lua` to turn them off entirely.
- **Hostile images and SVGs** can no longer hang, crash or exhaust Descry: an SVG dash pattern that looped forever, a quadratic text scan, giant declared image sizes, and unbounded text and font caches.
- **Plugins** run confined:
  - no processes, no native modules, no bytecode and no `debug` library;
  - files only inside the open vault and the plugin folder.
  - See [docs/plugins.md](https://github.com/fezcode/Descry/blob/main/docs/plugins.md#sandbox).
- **Vault safety:** symlinks are followed only when they stay inside the vault, and a vault's old `.descry.state` file can only reopen that vault's own notes.
- **HTML export** adds a strict Content-Security-Policy and drops `javascript:` links, so an exported page runs no script.
- **Builds** gain a stack protector, `_FORTIFY_SOURCE`, and PIE with full RELRO on Linux. On Windows, run-time DLLs load only from the app folder and System32.
- **Release pipeline:** actions are pinned by commit, the build token is read-only, linuxdeploy is pinned and checksummed, and releases now include `SHA256SUMS.txt`.

## README badges render

Descry rasterizes SVG with nanosvg, which is a shape rasterizer: it has no
handler for `<text>`, `<image>` or `<clipPath>` and silently drops all three.
That is most of a shields.io badge, so a README's badges showed up as bare
colour bars — no labels, no logos, square corners.

A new second pass (`src/svg_extra.c`) composites what nanosvg leaves out:

- **Labels** — `<text>` shaped with HarfBuzz and rasterized with FreeType,
  through the full transform chain, honouring `text-anchor` and `textLength`
  (the mechanism a badge uses to make its label fit its box). `font-family`
  lists resolve against a per-OS table, with synthetic bold/oblique when a
  variant is missing.
- **Logos** — `<image>` data URIs (`image/svg+xml`, base64 or percent-encoded)
  rasterized as nested SVG.
- **Rounded corners** — the `<clipPath>` rect as an antialiased mask, applied
  only when it covers the whole canvas, so a clip aimed at one sub-element can
  never erase the rest of the image.

### Also fixed

`load_svg` un-premultiplied a buffer `nsvgRasterize` had already
un-premultiplied. Dividing by alpha twice inflated every antialiased edge
pixel of every SVG; on a badge it pushed channels past 255 and wrapped them —
the cyan Go gopher rendered green.

### Tests

`tests/test_svg_extra.c` pins the parser against the real shields.io document
(transforms, colours, inheritance, `style=""` precedence, entities, tspans,
`<title>` exclusion, clipPath inside `<defs>`, truncated input). The parser
and compositor were also fuzzed with 75k mutated and garbage inputs against a
guard page.

### Windows Defender false positives

A freshly built `descry.exe` was being quarantined as
`Trojan:Win32/Bearfoos.A!ml` — an ML verdict on an unsigned binary with no
reputation, not a signature match. This release gives the classifier less to
work with and adds the durable fix:

- **VERSIONINFO** — the exe now carries a full company / product /
  description / version block. `src/version.h` owns the version string and
  CMake parses it back out, so the resource can't drift from the running app.
- **PE hardening** — linked with `--dynamicbase --high-entropy-va
  --nxcompat`. MinGW's `ld` leaves ASLR and DEP off by default.
- **Tighter plugin sandbox** — `os.execute`, `os.exit`, `io.popen` and
  `package.loadlib` are removed from the Lua host. Nothing in the documented
  plugin surface needs to spawn a process, load a DLL or take the app down.
  `io.open`, `os.time`, `os.date`, `os.getenv` and the rest stay.
- **Unstripped installer** — Forge no longer builds with `-s -w`.
- **Code signing** — `tools/sign.ps1` Authenticode-signs from
  `DESCRY_SIGN_THUMBPRINT` / `DESCRY_SIGN_PFX`, and `build.ps1 -Sign` routes
  the exe and installer through it. `tools/make-dev-cert.ps1` mints a local

## Modal inputs scroll with the caret
The one-line input in the **folder picker**, the **rename popup** and the **prompt modal** drew its text at a fixed origin inside a clip rect. Type a path wider than the field and the caret — along with everything after it — was drawn outside the clip and simply disappeared; you were stuck looking at the head of the path with no way to see what you were typing.

The view now follows the caret. Walk right and the text slides under it; `Home` scrolls back to the start, `End` returns to the tail, and the caret always lands inside the field's padding rather than under its border. Selection highlighting moves with it.

The scroll math lives in a new pure `inputfield.c` — a `clamp` + `follow` pair in the same shape as the tab strip's, so the caret (which sits one glyph-width past the end of the string) can't be clamped half outside the field. `tests/test_inputfield.c` pins it: clamp bounds, short text that never scrolls, the caret at either end, an already-visible caret leaving the view alone, and a shrinking string re-clamping instead of parking in empty space.

The settings card sized itself from the row count alone and never consulted the window height, so in a short window the tail of the list — and the hint line under it — ran off the bottom edge with nothing to scroll and no way to reach them.

# Gitland 0.14.0

## Windows release

Download and run **Gitland-Setup-0.14.0.exe**. The installer places Gitland in `%LOCALAPPDATA%\Programs\Gitland`, creates the shortcuts you select, and registers an uninstall entry in Apps & Features. The .NET runtime is included.

## Every repository in one place

A **Workspace** entry now sits at the top of the navigation rail. Point it at the folder your repositories live in and every one of them appears in a single table, so the question "what have I left unfinished?" is answered by looking rather than by opening eight repositories in turn.

The folder is chosen once and remembered. Only repositories directly inside it are listed; a repository nested deeper is not, which keeps the scan to one directory read rather than a walk of your whole disk. A linked worktree or a submodule checkout carries `.git` as a file instead of a folder, and both are listed.

### What a row tells you

| Column | Shows |
| --- | --- |
| Repository | The folder name |
| Branch | The current branch, or `HEAD (detached)` |
| Changes | `clean`, or `+` new, `~` modified, `−` deleted, `!` conflicted |
| Sync | `↑` commits waiting to push, `↓` commits waiting to pull |
| Remotes | How many remotes are configured, or `local` for none |

Conflicts get their own count rather than being folded into "modified". Gitland is a merge client, and a repository stopped mid-merge is not the same as one with edits in it.

A repository that cannot be read — a broken `gitdir`, a folder Git refuses on ownership grounds — keeps its row and shows the reason. One unreadable folder never blanks the table.

### Narrowing the list

Filter by name, or switch to **Unclean** or **Clean**. Unclean means uncommitted work *or* commits not yet exchanged with the remote, so a repository with a spotless working tree and three unpushed commits still counts. That is the reading `atlas.radar --show unclean` uses, and it is the one that answers the question the table is for. The context bar keeps the running total: *4 of 8 need attention*.

Choosing a row opens that repository. Right-clicking one offers Open, Reveal in File Explorer, Copy path, and a fetch for that repository alone.

### Acting on all of them

**Fetch all** brings the `↑`/`↓` counts up to date without touching a branch or a working tree, so it simply runs. **Pull all** and **Push all** change history or publish it, so each one first names every repository it would touch and does nothing at all unless you confirm:

- Pull skips repositories with uncommitted changes, and says how many it skipped.
- Push covers only repositories that have somewhere to push and something to send.
- Neither ever forces.

All three respect the filter currently applied, so narrowing to one project's repositories and fetching covers those and no others.

### Staying current

While the view is open, the folder is watched. A commit you make in another tool updates its row on its own: an event is matched back to the repository it happened in, and only that row is re-read, after the burst of writes settles. Leaving the view stops the watching, so the diff and merge views pay nothing for it. F5 rescans everything.

## Two fixes for Git 2.55

Both of these are long-standing faults that a recent Git turned into visible ones.

**Bisect never reported its answer.** Git 2.55 prints `is the first 'bad' commit`, quoting the term where earlier releases did not. Gitland matched only the unquoted wording, so a bisect that had found its commit reported nothing and simply looked stuck.

**Stash left untracked files behind.** Gitland passes `--literal-pathspecs` to Git so that a file whose name contains pathspec syntax is treated as a name. Under Git 2.55 that flag stops `git stash push --include-untracked` from removing the untracked files it has just stashed: the stash held them, the working tree still held them too, and the checkout was reported clean. The stash command passes no pathspec of its own, so the flag protected nothing there and is no longer applied to it.

Each row is two Git processes, so a folder of forty repositories would start eighty. The installer places Gitland in `%LOCALAPPDATA%\Programs\Gitland`, creates the shortcuts you select, and registers an uninstall entry in Apps & Features. The .NET runtime is included. Git must be installed and on PATH; GitHub actions also require the GitHub CLI and authentication.

## You can undo your changes

Until now Gitland could only move a change between the working tree and the index. It could never throw one away, which left stash as the only exit. That gap is closed, and it is closed the way the rest of Gitland treats destructive work — nothing is lost silently.

- **Discard** a single hunk, a whole file, or every change in the repository, and delete untracked files.
- Discarding from the unstaged view keeps what you have already staged; discarding from the staged view returns the file to its last commit.
- Before anything is removed, tracked work is snapshotted into a commit recorded under **Repository → Recovery**, and untracked files are copied into the Git directory's `gitland-backups` folder. Both are restorable.
- **Hard reset** joins soft and mixed, recording both the abandoned commit and the overwritten working tree.

## Everyday operations that were missing

- **Amend** can now fold the staged index into the last commit, not just rewrite its message.
- **Unstage a hunk**, the counterpart to hunk staging.
- **Forced push** using `--force-with-lease`, so amending or rebasing no longer leaves you unable to push, and a teammate's commits are still never overwritten.
- **Pull** runs fast-forward, merge, or rebase, and can stash your changes first instead of refusing to run.
- **Fetch** can prune deleted remote branches.
- **History search** by message or author now runs in Git, so a match older than the loaded page is found instead of missed.
- **File history** for the selected file.

## Investigate and rewrite

- **Interactive rebase.** Reorder commits, and set each to pick, reword, edit, squash, fixup, or drop. The plan is validated before it runs and handed to Git directly, so no editor opens and a plan that could not finish is refused rather than abandoned half-way.
- **Blame** for the selected file, and **reflog** browsing.
- **Bisect** with good, bad, and skip.
- **Cherry-pick a run** of commits, and **revert a merge commit** by choosing which parent to keep.
- **Take ours or theirs** for a whole conflicted file, without opening the merge editor.

## Previously out of scope

- **Submodules**: add, update, and sync.
- **Git LFS**: read and edit tracked patterns.
- **Hooks** listing, **commit signature verification**, **patch** export and apply, and **archive** a revision as a zip.
- **Move or rename** a tracked file, and **add a pattern to .gitignore**.
- **GitHub Enterprise** hosts, replacing the hardcoded github.com.

## Also

The open repository is watched, so edits made in your editor appear without pressing F5. Refreshes are coalesced and never run while a merge result has unsaved edits.

## Validation

- Release build: zero warnings and errors.
- 149 core and real Git integration tests passed, including 45 covering the operations above against real repositories.
- 190 offscreen native UI checks passed.
- Setup verified as a GUI-subsystem executable and reported with its SHA-256 checksum.

## Upgrading

Discard snapshots are ordinary Git objects and ordinary files. They survive restarts, but `git gc` prunes unreachable recovery refs on its own schedule and deleting the repository deletes both. Treat discard as recoverable for the session, not as an archive.

Two features that pull in the same direction: how the type lands on the page, and what the backspace key does to it.

## Struck type

Text is no longer drawn a line at a time. Every character is placed individually, and each one sits a hair off the line and carries its own amount of ink — the way a typebar does when it hits a platen. About one character in twenty-five comes out light, the way a key does when the ribbon is tired.

The variation is derived from the line and column rather than from a running random number, so a given cell always strikes the same way. The page does not shimmer between redraws, and scrolling never reshuffles the ink — it is the same impression you typed, every time you come back to it.

It is also **cheaper than what it replaced**. Glyphs now come from a cache of one texture per printable ASCII character, tinted and faded as they are blitted, so a redraw allocates nothing at all and changing theme costs nothing. The whole-line render this replaces built a fresh surface *and* texture for every visible line, on every frame.

On by default. Turn it off with **Strike variation** in the Options menu (`Ctrl+K`), or in the Hisashi **View** menu, and text renders dead straight at uniform ink. Persisted as `strike_variation=`.

## Carriage backspace

Off by default. Turn on **Carriage backspace** and the key stops erasing, and starts doing what it does on a typewriter: it runs the carriage back over the ink without lifting any of it, and stops dead at the left margin — ringing the bell rather than reaching up to the line above.

Because a typewriter has no insert, the mode also makes typing overstrike. A key struck over an occupied column lands on top of what is already there, and the character that was there stays visible underneath, drawn faintly and off by a pixel. Type `cat`, backspace three times, type `xxx`, and you get three double impressions rather than clean replacement — which is how you cross a word out on a real machine.

### Behaviour
- The ghosts are **cosmetic and one strike deep**. They are never written to the file, copied to the clipboard or matched by Find — the buffer holds exactly the characters you last struck.
- Any edit that rearranges a line structurally, such as splitting it or deleting a selection, simply drops them.
- **The escape hatch is always there.** `Delete` still erases forward, selecting text and typing still replaces it, and `Ctrl+Z` still undoes an overstrike and puts the original character back.
- The status bar shows `OVR` while the mode is on.
- Persisted as `carriage_backspace=`.

**Paper effects** — the page can now carry the marks of having been used. Off by default: turn on **Paper effects** in the Options menu (`Ctrl+K`), or in the Hisashi **View** menu.

### What lands on the page
- **Coffee rings** — two of them, elliptical, as if the cup sat at an angle. The dark tide line where the puddle dried sits just inside the rim, with a fainter second ring from an earlier drink further in.
- **Ink spills** — four lobed blots with a solid core and a definite edge, not a smudge.
- **Creases** — three folds, each with a sharp core and a broad band of shading beside it, shadowed on one side and catching the light on the other.
- **Grain** — the tooth of the paper itself, across the whole sheet.

### Drawn on noise, not on curves
Everything is generated from multi-octave value noise rather than smooth analytic falloffs. A Gaussian edge and a few sine harmonics on a circle are still a circle: the first attempt looked printed rather than spilled. So the ring rim wanders on noise, and its density varies around the circumference — reaching zero often enough to break the ring open, the way a drying puddle actually leaves it.

### Behaviour
- The marks are composited **under the text**, so a stain never competes with what you have written.
- Each theme carries its own colours for each kind of mark — a brown ring would be invisible on Terminal Green.
- The seed is fixed, so this is the same sheet of paper every launch rather than a fresh mess each time.
- It is one texture, rebuilt only on a window resize or a theme change — never per frame. Idle CPU is unchanged.
- Persisted as `paper_effects=` in `typewriter.ini`.
